shots.narration: Every ocean Earth has ever had, one night each,
and Doug gets a time machine, a snorkel and one job: last until sunrise.
Doug did not agree to this.
Paleozoic.
Anomalocaris.
Five hundred and eight million years ago, this was the biggest hunter in the sea,
and it could see you coming from a long way off.
It grew to somewhere between sixty centimeters and a meter long,
about the size of a skateboard, which in the Cambrian made it a giant.
It had two spiny grabbing arms in front of its mouth
and two huge eyes, each with at least sixteen thousand lenses,
giving it eyesight close to a modern dragonfly's.
Below it, the seafloor was covered in trilobites, which wore armor,
and for years scientists blamed Anomalocaris for the bite-shaped scars on their shells.
Here's the twist.
It probably couldn't crack them.
In twenty twenty-three, a team built a digital model of those grabbing arms
and tested them the way engineers test a bridge.
The arms were fast and very good at grabbing,
but a hard shell would have damaged them,
and trilobites built their shells from minerals, almost like rock.
So Anomalocaris most likely left the armor alone
and hunted soft, fast animals swimming in the bright water above the seafloor.
Doug hides among the trilobites
and knocks on a shell to check.
Everything down here is armored,
except the one animal wearing a snorkel.
Doug has died.
Again.
In a sea full of armor, the most dangerous thing you could possibly be was soft.
Endoceras.
About four hundred and sixty million years ago, one of the most dangerous shapes in the ocean
was a very long, very straight cone.
Endoceras was a nautiloid, an ancient cousin of today's nautilus,
and it lived in a long, straight shell divided into chambers,
with its tentacles reaching out of the open end.
It may have been one of the top predators of its time.
It hunted close to the seafloor,
and the big adults probably lay still and waited for prey to come to them.
The biggest Endoceras fossil is a piece of shell three meters long,
kept in a museum at Harvard University, and it's missing its tip.
When scientists filled in the missing part,
they got a full length of about five point seven meters.
That's about as long as a big pickup truck.
But here's the problem.
Nearly half of that length is an estimate.
It depends on how long the missing end used to be,
and a twenty twenty-five study warned that its own guess might be on the generous side.
There were also old reports of ten-meter shells,
but nobody ever collected or photographed them,
and most Endoceras were much smaller than the record holder anyway.
Doug finds an empty old shell and climbs inside.
An Endoceras lies beside him all night,
waiting for something to swim past.
Doug never swims past.
Doug is fine.
The biggest shell of its time is three meters of fossil and nearly three meters of educated guessing.
Jaekelopterus.
Sea scorpions sound like something made up for a monster film,
but this one is real.
It's the largest sea scorpion ever found, and one of the two biggest arthropods in history.
Arthropods are the huge group that includes insects, spiders, crabs and lobsters.
About four hundred million years ago, in what is now Germany,
Jaekelopterus hunted in a shallow lagoon or river delta, where the water was probably not fully salty.
In two thousand and seven, scientists described a single claw found in a German quarry.
Part of it was broken off, but complete, it would have been about forty-six centimeters long.
That's about the length of a computer keyboard,
and it's only the claw.
Here's the unsettling part.
For this giant, the claw is all we have.
Everything else was scaled up from it, using the body proportions of its closest relatives.
The answer was a body about two and a half meters long,
longer than a grown man lying down,
and the claws stuck out roughly another meter in front of that.
Its only real rival for the record is Arthropleura,
a giant millipede relative that lived on land, and the size estimates for the two are very close.
For comparison, the arthropod with the biggest leg span alive today, the Japanese spider crab,
is mostly legs.
Doug treats it like a lobster in a restaurant tank,
taps on the water and says hello.
There is no glass.
The whole animal was rebuilt from one claw,
and honestly, the claw on its own would have been enough.
Dunkleosteus.
Most fish have teeth,
but Dunkleosteus didn't need any, because the edges of its jaws were sharp blades of bone.
It lived about three hundred and sixty million years ago, in a shallow sea that covered what is now Ohio,
and its head and chest were wrapped in thick plates of armor.
In two thousand and six, two scientists built a computer model of its jaw
and estimated a bite force of more than four thousand four hundred newtons at the tip.
That's roughly the weight of a grand piano pressing down on a single point.
It was also fast.
The model suggested it could open its mouth in about one fiftieth of a second,
quick enough to suck prey straight in.
Most fish have either a strong bite or a fast bite,
and Dunkleosteus had both.
But that's not the worst news.
In twenty twenty-three, scientists shrank it.
Older books said it could reach about nine meters long.
A new study, based on the proportions of its head, cut a typical adult down to about three point four meters,
a bit shorter than a small car.
The same study made it far chunkier, though,
with a body shaped like a tuna's and a huge mouth.
Doug has seen this fish before.
It was dying at the time,
so Doug waves at it like it's a school reunion.
Science took nearly six meters off Dunkleosteus
and somehow made it more dangerous.
Helicoprion.
In eighteen ninety-nine, a geologist in Russia described a fossil shaped like a spiral of teeth,
and for the next century, nobody could say where it went.
The spiral is called a tooth whorl.
New teeth grew at one end while the older ones rolled toward the middle,
so the whole thing kept coiling up for the animal's entire life.
One whorl found at a mine in Idaho is about twenty centimeters across, a little smaller than a basketball.
The biggest whorls point to an animal around six to seven and a half meters long.
The rest of the body was made of cartilage, which rarely fossilizes,
so scientists had a spiral of teeth and no idea where to put it.
Here comes the strange part.
The first reconstruction put the spiral on the end of its nose, curled back over the head.
Later guesses put it on the tail,
on the back fin,
hanging under the chin, or deep down in the throat.
The answer finally came in twenty thirteen, when researchers ran X-ray scans on a fossil in an Idaho museum
that had first been described in nineteen sixty-six.
The whorl filled the middle of the lower jaw like a circular saw,
and there were no teeth at all in the upper jaw.
The scans also showed it wasn't a true shark.
Its closest living relatives are ratfish, which live in the deep sea today.
Doug holds up the three old drawings,
studies them carefully, and tries to guess which one is right.
He picks the tail.
It took scientists a hundred and fourteen years to find the jaw,
and it took Doug fourteen minutes.
Mesozoic.
Cymbospondylus.
After the worst mass extinction in Earth's history, the ocean was close to empty,
but it did not stay that way for long.
Cymbospondylus was an ichthyosaur, a sea reptile shaped a little like a dolphin.
In twenty eleven, a team in the mountains of Nevada dug up its skull, part of its backbone and a front flipper.
Freeing the bones from the rock took the better part of three years.
The skull alone is about two meters long,
and the whole animal is estimated at more than seventeen meters.
That's about a city bus and a half.
It hunted in a sea full of squid-like ammonites and small eel-like animals called conodonts.
Researchers think that food supply, filling the empty space the extinction left behind,
is what let ichthyosaurs grow so big.
The incredible part is how fast it happened.
Cymbospondylus lived only about three million years after the first ichthyosaurs appeared,
while whales took far longer to reach their biggest sizes.
As far as scientists know, it was the first truly giant animal ever to live on Earth.
Doug arrives at sunset with a hopeful hand-painted sign.
The ocean is recovering, it says.
The sign was right.
The ocean had recovered,
and the first thing it built was big enough to swallow the man holding the sign.
Pliosaurus.
If you grew up on nature documentaries,
you might remember a sea reptile twenty-five meters long,
and that one was wrong.
In nineteen ninety-nine, a famous television series showed its relative Liopleurodon as a twenty-five-meter monster.
The scientist who advised on it later said the number came from scraps of fossil,
and a study published in twenty twenty-six puts Liopleurodon at just over eight meters, tops.
So the TV version shrank by about two thirds.
Then there's Pliosaurus.
About a hundred and fifty-five million years ago, off what is now the coast of Dorset, England,
one of them left behind a skull more than two meters long.
That's about as tall as a front door,
and it's only the head.
A computer model of that skull found that its strongest bites came from the back of the jaws,
between six thousand and eleven thousand pounds of force.
It probably grabbed prey, worked it to the back of its mouth, and crushed it there.
However, the model found one weakness.
Twisting or shaking big prey could have damaged its own skull,
so it probably didn't shake its food at all.
It just bit harder.
Now for the part the size correction left out.
In twenty twenty-two, another nearly complete pliosaur skull came out of a Dorset cliff,
about two meters long and holding a hundred and thirty teeth,
with a bite far stronger than a crocodile's.
The fossil hunter who dug it out believes the rest of the animal is still inside that cliff.
And the cliff is wearing away.
Doug reads about the size correction and relaxes,
floating on his back with his snorkel off.
He is reading about the wrong animal.
The correction made Liopleurodon smaller,
but it did nothing about the two-meter head in the water underneath Doug.
Xiphactinus.
About eighty-five million years ago, Kansas was underwater,
and one of the scariest things in it was a fish with an underbite full of fangs.
A shallow sea ran through the middle of North America back then, and Xiphactinus hunted in it.
It could reach about five meters long,
and it could swallow a two-meter fish whole.
We know that because of one famous fossil.
In nineteen fifty-two, a fossil hunter named George Sternberg dug up a Xiphactinus about four meters long.
Inside its ribcage was another fish, called Gillicus, nearly two meters long,
which is about as long as a grown man is tall.
The fossil was so big that it didn't fit on his truck
and had to be sawed in half to move it.
Today it hangs in the Sternberg Museum in Hays, Kansas,
and it's the most photographed fossil in their collection.
The disturbing part is the timing.
The bones of the Gillicus were never digested.
That means the big fish died soon after its meal.
The usual reading is that the meal itself was the problem,
and that Xiphactinus took on more than it could survive.
At sunset, a Xiphactinus finds Doug
and swallows him whole.
Then it does what its species is famous for,
and gives up.
Doug climbs out at sunrise.
Doug is fine.
The narrator had already written a death here.
For Xiphactinus, a big meal could be its last meal.
This time, the meal swam home.
Tylosaurus.
Mosasaurs were giant sea lizards that lived alongside the dinosaurs,
and Tylosaurus was one of the biggest of them all.
It patrolled the same Kansas sea as Xiphactinus.
The largest individuals are estimated at around thirteen or fourteen meters long,
which is longer than a city bus.
We know what it ate.
In nineteen eighteen, a fossil collector named Charles Sternberg found a Tylosaurus
with the bones of a young plesiosaur, a long-necked sea reptile, inside its ribcage.
Other Tylosaurus fossils show it also ate fish, seabirds, sharks and smaller mosasaurs.
It was not a picky eater,
and it was about to meet a very easy meal.
The worst part is the roof of its mouth.
On top of the teeth lining its jaws, Tylosaurus had two extra rows of teeth on the roof of its mouth.
They pointed backward,
so once something was inside, those teeth helped move it toward the throat
and made it very hard to back out.
Doug has seen this idea before, on a moray eel.
Tylosaurus had the extra-large version.
Doug, fresh out of the last fish,
is now the only thing in this sea with no armor, no fins and a bright red hat.
The cap floats.
Inside one Tylosaurus, scientists found a plesiosaur.
Inside this one, they would find a snorkel.
Cenozoic.
Basilosaurus.
Basilosaurus means king lizard.
It is not a lizard,
and it was never anybody's king.
In eighteen thirty-four, the scientist who named it thought he'd found the bones of a giant sea reptile.
A few years later, another scientist looked closely at its teeth and realized it was a mammal, an early whale.
By then the name was stuck,
because under the rules of naming animals, the first name wins.
Basilosaurus lived between about thirty-eight and thirty-four million years ago.
One famous skeleton from the Valley of the Whales in Egypt
is about fifteen meters long, with a long, almost eel-like body.
And it still had legs.
Two tiny back legs stuck out of its sides, complete with knees, ankles and toes.
Each one was about the size of a three-year-old child's leg,
which is far too small to walk on.
Here comes the dark part.
In twenty nineteen, scientists studied what was preserved inside one of those skeletons.
They found the bones of young Dorudon, a smaller kind of whale, along with a large fish.
The Dorudon were so young they were probably still drinking milk,
and bite marks on their skulls pointed to hunting, not scavenging.
So Basilosaurus was a whale that hunted other whales.
Doug swims up beside it,
notices the tiny legs and laughs.
The rest of the animal notices Doug.
It had legs it couldn't use and a name it never earned,
and neither of those slowed it down.
Livyatan.
Today's sperm whales have teeth only in their lower jaw,
and they mostly suck in squid,
but their ancient cousin did something very different.
About ten million years ago, off the coast of what is now Peru,
Livyatan hunted with huge teeth in both its upper and lower jaws.
The biggest of them were up to thirty-six centimeters long.
That's longer than a school ruler.
Guinness lists them as the largest teeth any animal has used for eating,
and tusks don't count.
The whole animal is estimated at about thirteen and a half to seventeen and a half meters long,
and a newer study suggests it may have been a little smaller.
The scientists who described it think it most likely hunted medium-sized baleen whales,
which were packed with fat.
Its name comes from Leviathan, the sea monster in the Bible,
and from Herman Melville, who wrote Moby-Dick.
The team first called it Leviathan,
but that name already belonged to a fossil mastodon,
so they switched to the Hebrew spelling.
But that's not the scariest thing in this water.
Megalodon lived in the same region at the same time,
and its teeth turn up in the same area where Livyatan was found.
Doug has been clicked at by this whale's modern cousin before.
That cousin had no upper teeth.
This one has a full set.
Livyatan was named after a monster,
and it still wasn't the biggest predator in its own sea.
Megalodon.
Megalodon means giant tooth,
and teeth are almost all we have left of the biggest one.
Its skeleton, jaws included, was made of cartilage, which broke down after death,
so what survives is teeth and a few pieces of backbone.
The biggest teeth are more than eighteen centimeters long,
about as long as a grown man's hand.
Megalodon ruled the oceans from about twenty-three million years ago
until about three point six million years ago,
and its size has been argued about for decades.
One method, using the width of its teeth, gave a maximum of about twenty meters.
Then, in twenty twenty-five, a study used a fossil backbone from Belgium,
eleven meters long on its own,
to estimate that one shark at about sixteen meters.
Some even bigger vertebrae suggest it may have reached twenty-four meters,
which is two city buses parked end to end.
The same study argued Megalodon was slimmer than people usually draw it,
built more like a long, streamlined lemon shark than a bulky one.
It went after big prey.
A whale rib from North Carolina, three to four million years old,
carries three bite marks spaced to fit a Megalodon,
and that whale survived the bite.
The most disturbing part is where Megalodon sat on the food chain.
In twenty twenty-two, scientists measured nitrogen locked inside fossil shark teeth,
because the higher up the food chain an animal eats, the more of the heavy kind of nitrogen it carries.
Megalodon's score was the highest ever measured.
To score that high, it must have been eating predators,
and the predators that ate those predators.
Doug once climbed the whole ocean food chain.
Megalodon sat above the top of it.
So what finished it off?
A second study used zinc in fossil teeth
and found that early great white sharks were eating at nearly the same level,
which suggests competition may have played a part, although that's not proven.
